text:
US homeland security secretary Markwayne Mullin has defended his decision to fly in a private government to a college football game on Saturday as Americans weathered widespread flight delays and cancellations, saying: “We still got to live our life.”
Mullin, a former US senator from Oklahoma, traveled on a government aircraft on Saturday to watch a football game between Louisiana State University and the University of Texas, the New York Post reported on Tuesday. The trip to Baton Rouge, Louisiana, came about a day after a four-hour ground stop that led to thousands of flights being delayed or cancelled – and an estimated 1.5 million people were stranded.
Evidently, botched maintenance work upgrading telecommunication lines from old copper wire to fiber optic cables in at least one remote location prompted the FAA to implement the ground stop.
Mullin is required to travel on a government aircraft with secure communication systems and pay back the government for personal travel. Still, the homeland security secretary defended his decision to travel for pleasure while many other Americans were stranded.
“We would have never went if the airlines – if the airways – weren’t completely open. [And] they’d been completely open for 21 hours,” Mullin said on an interview on CNBC on Tuesday.
“I would have never taken airspace if the airspace wasn’t open and we still got to live our life at the same time.
“We still have family, friends, and we also have work we do every day.”
Mullin spent part of the game in the box of Ben Bordelon, CEO of Bollinger Shipping, a company that has Department of Homeland Security contracts, the Post reported. Mullin said on CNBC he did not know Bordelon.
He defended his travel as Republicans have sought to cast shift blame away from Donald Trump’s administration for the nationwide ground stop to Congress and the Joe Biden White House prior to Trump’s second presidency.
Democrats have said that characterization is “absurd”, noting that both the Biden administration and Congress have allocated tens of billions of dollars for air traffic control improvements.
